raw_case_text:
A 21-year-old Japanese male presented at the outpatient department with sporadic nausea, abdominal discomfort, and worsening headache. Cysto-peritoneal (CP) and VP shunts were implanted 11 months after birth by another doctor for the treatment of hydrocephalus due to a suprasellar arachnoid cyst. His VP shunt had been replaced twice by the age of 13 years. At the time of last surgery, the CP cranial tube was removed while the extra-cranial tube was left in place because it passed through the mediastinal space rather than the subcutaneous tissue and adhered to the surrounding organs. During this course of treatment, the patient had been diagnosed with slit ventricle syndrome but had no current restrictions on daily activity except for mild mental retardation. He had no remarkable medical history to suggest systemic abnormalities or risk factors for infection and had not traveled to foreign countries.
Nausea was reported for 2 months and abdominal pain for 1 month before admission. A few days before presentation, the patient developed fever and mild consciousness disturbance. Initial physical examination revealed a fever of 38.9 C, restlessness, and significant abdominal distension but no meningeal irritation or focal signs of neurological dysfunction. White blood cell count was 10,900/mm3, and serum C-reactive protein level was 31.8 mg/dl. Chest X-ray was negative but brain and abdominal computed tomography (CT) scans revealed enlarge lateral ventricles, a huge peritoneal cyst surrounding the distal end of the peritoneal tube, and fluid in the sheath surrounding the peritoneal tube, indicating possible shunt blockage and a concomitant increase in intracranial pressure (ICP) [Figure 1]. In contrast, chest CT revealed no abnormalities in bilateral lung fields or subcutaneous tissues of the chest. The tentative diagnosis was shunt malfunction resulting from some undefined peritoneal abnormality.
Continuous external drainage was established to remove CSF from the lateral ventricles and peritoneal cyst. The CSF was clear and the fluid in the abdominal cyst was xanthochromatic. Chemical screening of CSF was negative. The cyst fluid contained 1495 cells/mm3 (69 monocytes and 1426 polycytes/mm3) and 1.4 g/dl total protein. Antibiotic therapies for abdominal infection were empirically administered and bacterial cultures analyzed, but no causative pathogen was identified.
Preoperative clinical symptoms immediately improved after surgery to insert an external drainage system. However, the cyst fluid gradually recollected and signs of mild inflammation remained despite antibiotic therapy. In the second stage of treatment, transcutaneous drainage of the cyst under CT guidance was performed; however, again cyst fluid recollected [Figure 2]. In the third stage of treatment, laparotomy was performed, which revealed no membrane surrounding the abdominal cyst (defining it as a pseudocyst), no malignancies within the omentum, and no ascites within the abdominal cavity.
Throughout the course of treatment, all cytological examinations for malignancies were negative and bacterial cultures did not reveal a causative pathogen. Two months after initial surgery, inflammation of his left knee joint became apparent. The fluid taken from the joint was xanthochromatic, similar to the pseudocyst fluid, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis was detected in a culture from the fluid. Thus, the patient was diagnosed with an abdominal pseudocyst associated with TBP and successfully treated by anti-TB agents following insertion of a ventriculo-pleural shunt [Figure 3]. At follow-up 2 years after treatment, he again presented with signs of inflammation, and the abscess around the CP shunt was strongly suspected as the cause. He was again treated with anti-TB agents, and all signs of inflammation subsided after the removal of the previous CP shunt tube by thoracoscopic surgery.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 21-year-old Japanese male with congenital hydrocephalus and retained cystoperitoneal/ventriculoperitoneal shunts presented with 2 months of sporadic nausea, 1 month of abdominal pain and distension, worsening headache, fever, and mild disturbance of consciousness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed sporadic nausea 2 months prior and abdominal pain 1 month prior to admission, followed a few days before presentation by high fever (38.9 °C), worsening headache, abdominal distension, and mild obtundation.
subjective.past_medical_history: Suprasellar arachnoid cyst with hydrocephalus treated at 11 months of age with cystoperitoneal (CP) and ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunts; VP shunt revised twice by age 13 (with retention of the extracranial mediastinal/peritoneal CP catheter); slit-ventricle syndrome and mild intellectual disability. No foreign travel or known infectious risk factors.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for nausea, abdominal pain/distension, worsening headache, fever, restlessness, and later left knee joint swelling.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature 38.9 °C, restlessness/mild consciousness disturbance, and marked abdominal distension without neck stiffness or focal neurological deficits. Two months after initial abdominal surgery, he developed overt left knee arthritis/effusion.
objective.routine_investigations: WBC 10,900/mm^3, serum CRP 31.8 mg/dL, and normal chest X-ray.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain and abdominal CT demonstrated enlarged lateral ventricles, fluid tracking along the shunt sheath, and a massive abdominal peritoneal pseudocyst surrounding the distal VP shunt tip; chest CT was normal. Ventricular CSF was clear and chemically normal, while xanthochromic abdominal pseudocyst fluid showed 1,495 cells/mm^3 (1,426 polymorphs and 69 mononuclear cells/mm^3), total protein 1.4 g/dL, negative malignant cytology, and negative routine bacterial cultures. Because the abdominal collection recurred after external drainage, CT-guided percutaneous drainage, and laparotomy (which confirmed an unencapsulated peritoneal pseudocyst without omental malignancy), arthrocentesis of a newly inflamed left knee joint 2 months post-op yielded xanthochromic synovial fluid.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Culture of the xanthochromic left knee joint fluid isolated Mycobacterium tuberculosis, confirming tuberculous peritonitis (TBP)-associated abdominal VP shunt pseudocyst and tuberculous monoarthritis of the left knee. He was successfully treated with anti-tuberculous chemotherapy and conversion to a ventriculopleural shunt; when peri-shunt inflammation recurred 2 years later around the retained trans-mediastinal CP shunt tube, repeat anti-TB therapy and thoracoscopic removal of the retained CP catheter achieved permanent resolution.
